humanities_role_explanation: Designed to evaluate disciplinary competence in art history and aesthetics, employing a five-layer cultural understanding framework grounded in Panofsky's iconological method.
benchmark_modalities_explanation: Multimodal evaluation pairing historical artwork images with free-text generative expert critiques across eight cultural traditions.
analytical_tasks_explanation: Evaluates generative art critique across five hierarchical layers: visual perception (L1), technical analysis of medium and brushwork (L2), cultural and iconographical symbolism (L3), historical attribution/context (L4), and culture-specific philosophical aesthetics (L5).

general_purpose_benchmark.note: Scoped specifically to art-historical visual understanding and cross-cultural art critique.

evaluates_generative_llm.note: Evaluates several state-of-the-art vision-language models, including GPT-4o, Claude-Sonnet-4.5, Gemini-2.5-Pro, Qwen3-VL-235B, GLM-4V-Flash, and DeepSeek-VL2.

quantitative_metrics.note: Evaluates model performance using Dimension Coverage Rate (DCR), semantic embedding alignment, and human evaluation scores.

published_after_march_2023.note: Published as a preprint in February 2026.

summary: VULCA-BENCH is a multicultural art-critique benchmark of 7,410 image-critique pairs across eight traditions, designed to test vision-language models' deep cultural and philosophical understanding beyond surface-level perception. Grounded in a five-layer framework mapping from visual features to philosophical aesthetics, it enforces a 'Cultural Symmetry' principle to balance structural depth and representation across Western and non-Western traditions.
key_findings: All evaluated VLMs show a prominent 25–40 percentage-point decline (layer gap) from visual perception (L1-L2) to cultural and aesthetic interpretation (L3-L5). Naive few-shot learning actually degrades performance across most models, indicating that simple in-context prompting is insufficient to elicit deep cultural reasoning.
facets_explanation: The reference critiques and dimension tags were generated by domain-expert annotators (PhDs and MAs in art history), with all annotator-reviewer disagreements resolved through consensus discussion to ensure a single, highly accurate ground truth. Correctly interpreting the artworks at layers L3-L5 requires external historical and philosophical knowledge not contained in the visual stimuli. The pilot evaluation employs Dimension Coverage Rate (DCR) which matches the generated critique against a dictionary of culture-specific synonyms representing the target dimension set.
results_explanation: The paper reports a performance gap between difficulty regimes, specifically between visual perception (L1–L2) and cultural interpretation (L3–L5). The largest gap of 40 percentage points (40.3 pp unrounded) is reported for GPT-4o, which drops from '87.1' % on L1–L2 to '46.8' % on L3–L5 (Table 7). A quantified human baseline is not reported for comparison against the models on the primary metric, so the human gap is null. The best-performing model on the benchmark's primary diagnostic metric (Dimension Coverage Rate, which is classified as 'other') is Gemini-2.5-Pro, achieving a score of '72.4' on the Balanced-Pilot subset (Table 7) and '70.8' on the Full corpus (Table 9). Although the benchmark is multicultural, the paper evaluates models on an aggregate balanced pilot and does not report a systematic finding of cultural asymmetry for the evaluated models.
